lines: For the last few weeks, I've been building a software factory on top of Claude Code, <break time="0.3s" /> and running real requests through it.

In this video, I'll show you how it works. <break time="0.4s" /> Where it came from, <break time="0.2s" /> what makes it different from just using agents, <break time="0.2s" /> what's under the hood... <break time="0.3s" /> and one real request, from the issue, all the way to a merge request. <break time="0.5s" /> If you already use Claude Code, this is the next step.

So... <break time="0.5s" /> you already use Claude Code. <break time="0.5s" /> Now imagine you stop driving every session yourself, and instead, you build a factory that does it for you. <break time="0.4s" /> Let me show you what that actually looks like.

AI coding has evolved in three steps. <break time="0.4s" /> First, on your laptop, where you prompt, Claude edits, and you check every change yourself. <break time="0.4s" /> Then came remote agents. You type a prompt in the Claude app, even on your phone, and the work happens in the cloud. <break time="0.4s" /> And alongside them, something different appeared: factories. <break time="0.4s" /> A factory isn't about where the agent runs. It's about how the work is organised.

Put them side by side. <break time="0.4s" /> Local and remote agents differ mostly in where they run. <break time="0.4s" /> A factory changes who decides what gets built, who checks it, and what gets recorded. <break time="0.4s" /> You approve the requirements before anything is built, a separate agent checks the work, and every check leaves evidence behind.

The definition I like best comes from Dru Knox, at Tessl. <break time="0.3s" /> A software factory is any agentic system where agents write all of the code you ship. <break time="0.4s" /> Which means your job changes. You stop building the product... and you start building the machine that builds it.

So how do you know if your factory is any good? <break time="0.3s" /> Knox uses three measures, and the order matters. <break time="0.3s" /> First, autonomy. How often does a person have to step in and nudge the agents? <break time="0.3s" /> Then automation. How much can you let run without anyone reviewing it? <break time="0.3s" /> And then quality. You earn automation, by proving autonomy first.

And what makes autonomy safe? <break time="0.3s" /> Verification. <break time="0.4s" /> You can only stop reading every line if something else is checking it. Every time. And leaving a record you can actually inspect. <break time="0.4s" /> Without that, honestly, a factory is just a faster way to ship mistakes.

Now, a factory runs in three loops. <break time="0.3s" /> The inner loop is where agents iterate before anything goes up for review. It's fast, and it's cheap. <break time="0.3s" /> The outer loop is the slower, thorough checking, the kind that replaces your review time. <break time="0.3s" /> And then there's the meta loop. That one watches the corrections and the failures... and fixes the factory itself, so the same mistake doesn't happen twice.

Okay. Here's the factory I built, on top of Claude Code. <break time="0.3s" /> It has eleven stages. Agents write the requirements, the plan, and the code. <break time="0.3s" /> Scripts do everything that can be checked mechanically. <break time="0.3s" /> And a person steps in exactly twice.

And here's the thing. <break time="0.4s" /> The whole pipeline is just data. <break time="0.4s" /> Each stage says who does the work, an agent, a script, or a human, which skill it follows, and what it's allowed to write. <break time="0.4s" /> If a stage fails three times, the factory stops, and asks a person.

Every kind of job has a skill. <break time="0.3s" /> It's just a short, written instruction. <break time="0.4s" /> This one's for UI logic. Pure functions, no DOM, no clock. <break time="0.5s" /> And look at the last line. <break time="0.3s" /> The maker never ticks its own task, and never writes its own evidence.
Alright. <break time="0.5s" /> Let's watch one real request, <break time="0.2s" /> go all the way through.
It starts as a plain GitLab issue, <break time="0.2s" /> with the factory label on it. <break time="0.4s" /> A webhook kicks off a pass, straight away.
Within about a minute, the requirements are written. <break time="0.4s" /> And then the factory stops... and waits for a person.
The requirements are user stories, with acceptance criteria. <break time="0.3s" /> Everything downstream gets checked against these, so this approval actually means something.
Approving is one word on the issue. <break time="0.3s" /> Oh, and no slash. GitLab quietly swallows a comment that's only slash approve.
Next, <break time="0.3s" /> comes the plan. <break time="0.4s" /> The work is split into sections, <break time="0.2s" /> and every section ends with a gate, that the checker has to pass.

And these are the checker's gates. <break time="0.6s" /> They're written into the plan before any code exists. Real commands, with expected results. <break time="0.6s" /> The module's exports, no DOM access, the currency formatting, totals right down to the cent.

This is the inner loop in action. <break time="0.3s" /> A maker session builds a section. Then a completely separate checker session, one that never saw the maker work, runs the gate. <break time="0.4s" /> If it passes, the next section starts. If it fails... a fresh maker gets the written findings.
The checker writes down its evidence. <break time="0.4s" /> What it ran, what it expected, and what it actually found. <break time="0.5s" /> In this run... four sections, four passes, first time.
Then, <break time="0.3s" /> the outer loop kicks in. <break time="0.4s" /> A script re-runs the checks instead of trusting them, the full test suite runs, <break time="0.2s" /> and a preview goes up.
Now, <break time="0.4s" /> the person who asked for it gets to try the real thing, <break time="0.3s" /> right in a browser. <break time="0.6s" /> And they approve... again.
And then a merge request opens, with the specs and every bit of evidence linked. <break time="0.3s" /> Merging is still a human's call.

So how does it actually run? <break time="0.6s" /> An issue or a comment in GitLab fires a webhook, and that starts a pipeline on a runner. <break time="0.6s" /> Each pass pulls the factory's state from a git branch, walks the stages, and runs claude dash p for every agent step. <break time="0.6s" /> Then it pushes the work, comments on the issue, and saves its state again. <break time="0.6s" /> Nothing runs on your laptop.

Mapped back to the loops... the inner loop is maker and checker, per section, with three attempts. <break time="0.3s" /> The outer loop is scripts and tests, and then a person tries it. <break time="0.3s" /> And the meta loop? Every time someone has to step in, it's recorded, and the fix goes into a skill or a rule. <break time="0.4s" /> Honestly... right now, that loop is me. By hand.

Here are the numbers from that run. <break time="0.3s" /> Seventeen minutes from issue to merge request, approvals included. <break time="0.2s" /> Ten agent sessions. <break time="0.2s" /> About a dollar and twenty cents at API prices. <break time="0.3s" /> And every single section passed its checker the first time.

Now, the limits. <break time="0.6s" /> Checks prove the checks pass... not that the spec was right. That's exactly why a person approves the spec. <break time="0.6s" /> The meta loop is still manual. The runner handles one request at a time. <break time="0.6s" /> And it works best on small, clear requests.

Want to try it yourself? <break time="0.5s" /> There's a playground. <break time="0.3s" /> Your own GitLab project, with nothing to install. <break time="0.4s" /> File an issue, and watch it go through. <break time="0.5s" /> The code is open source, <break time="0.2s" /> and there's a longer write up on Medium.
